H1.text: Multiply a plus b by itself. Easy. You get three terms.

H2.text: Multiply it three times, and it takes longer. Now there are four terms.

H3.text: Aarav's homework tonight asks for a plus b, to the power ten.

H4.text: Ten brackets, multiplied one by one. That is a whole page of work. Is there a shortcut?

H5.text: There is. One line gives the whole answer. It is called the binomial theorem.

D2.text: A binomial is an expression with two parts, like a plus b. Bi means two.

D3.text: The power tells you how many brackets to multiply. a plus b, to the power three, means three brackets side by side.

P1.text: Now watch the brackets multiply. From each bracket, you pick one part: a or b.

P2.text: Pick a, a, a, and you get a cubed. Pick a, a, b, and you get a squared b.

P3.text: Every different pick makes one piece. Three brackets, two choices each. That makes eight picks.

P4.text: Now sort the pieces. One pick gives a cubed. Three picks give a squared b. Three give a b squared. One gives b cubed.

P5.text: So a plus b, cubed, is a cubed, plus three a squared b, plus three a b squared, plus b cubed.

C1.text: Here is the key question. Why are there three picks that give a squared b?

C2.text: Because you only decide which bracket gives the b. It can be the first, the second, or the third.

C3.text: Choosing r things out of n is exactly n C r, from the combinations episode. Here, three C one is three.

C4.text: So every number in front of a term is an n C r. It simply counts the ways to choose the brackets that give b.

L1.text: Now let the power grow. Watch n count up from one to ten.

L2.text: Each new power adds one more term. The numbers in front grow fast, and they always rise and fall evenly, like a hill.

L3.text: At n equals ten, they are one, ten, forty five, one hundred twenty, two hundred ten, two hundred fifty two, and then back down.

L4.text: Add them all, and you get one thousand and twenty four. That is two to the power ten.

G1.text: Now we can write the theorem in one line.

G2.text: Step one. The first term is a to the power n. Its number is n C zero, which is one.

G3.text: Step two. Each next term swaps one a for one b. The power of a goes down by one. The power of b goes up by one.

G4.text: Step three. In front of a to the n minus r, times b to the r, sits n C r. That is the number of ways to choose r brackets for b.

G5.text: Step four. The last term is b to the power n, with n C n, which is also one.

G6.text: So there are n plus one terms. And in every term, the two powers add up to n.

S1.text: Side by side. Many people think a plus b, squared, is just a squared plus b squared.

S2.text: Look at a square with side a plus b. It splits into four pieces. a squared, b squared, and two rectangles, each a times b.

S3.text: So a plus b, squared, is a squared, plus two a b, plus b squared. The middle term is what the shortcut forgets.

S4.text: Now you try. Is a plus b, cubed, equal to a cubed plus b cubed? Pause and decide.

S5.text: No! The middle terms, three a squared b and three a b squared, are missing. Only the first and the last terms match.

T1.text: Remember this. Pick one part from every bracket, and n C r counts the ways.

V1.text: Two quick tricks come straight out of the theorem.

V2.text: Trick one. a minus b is a plus minus b. Odd powers of minus b are negative, so the signs go plus, minus, plus, minus.

V3.text: Trick two. Put a equal to one, and b equal to x. You get one plus x, to the power n.

V4.text: Now put x equal to one. The left side becomes two to the n. The right side becomes all the n C r added up. So every row adds up to two to the n.

V5.text: Quick one. How many terms does a plus b, to the power ten, have? Ten, or eleven? Pause and think.

V6.text: Eleven! There is always one more term than the power, because r runs from zero all the way up to n.

W2.text: Expand x plus two, to the power four.

W3.text: Step one. n is four, so the numbers are four C zero up to four C four. One, four, six, four, one.

W4.text: Step two. The powers of x go down from four to zero. The powers of two go up from zero to four.

W5.text: Step three. Multiply each column. One x to the four. Four times x cubed times two, eight x cubed. Six times x squared times four, twenty four x squared.

W6.text: Then four times x times eight, thirty two x. And one times sixteen, sixteen.

W7.text: Check it with x equal to one. Three to the four is eighty one, and one plus eight plus twenty four plus thirty two plus sixteen is also eighty one.

X2.text: Expand x minus two, to the power four. Many students copy the last answer and turn every plus into a minus.

X3.text: But only odd powers of minus two are negative. Minus two, squared, is plus four. So the signs alternate: plus, minus, plus, minus, plus.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main, as questions that ask for an expansion, or for the sum of all the coefficients, which you get by putting x equal to one.

Q1.text: Exam level now. How many terms does this expansion have? Pause and solve.

A2.text: Put x equal to one. The coefficients add up to one plus two, to the power n. That is three to the n.

A3.text: Three to the n is six thousand five hundred sixty one. Three to the eight is exactly that, so n is eight.

A4.text: There is always one more term than the power. So the expansion has nine terms, not eight.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is a plus b, squared, not just a squared plus b squared?

Y3.text: Two. How many terms does a plus b, to the power seven, have?

Y4.text: Three. What do the coefficients of one plus x, to the power five, add up to?

N1.text: Next time: you need only the seventh term of a long expansion. Can you jump straight to it? We find out with the general term.
